title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: Quinta — non mortuus prout minatus
pass_a_gloss: Fifth reason finally (for it will be better to put off the rest and transfer them to another place). If the law was threatening Adam with death situated in privation of justice, Adam (as you assert) died just as God had threatened. But that seems false to me. For first, you, I suppose, confess that that first sin was forgiven to Adam, otherwise numbering him among the damned: he did not therefore die just as God had threatened. For these two fight each other, that sin be forgiven and that one be punished according to the law. Next, by the death denounced in the threat you understand both the death of the body and the eternal, as well as that spiritual one. It belonged therefore equally to the truth of the threat and to justice that, on the day he violated the law, on the same he should die both by bodily and eternal death and by spiritual. Yet on the same day he suffered neither, and the eternal he never underwent, nor will undergo. Why could not the punishment of spiritual death equally with eternal be forgiven to Adam? or at least deferred?
pass_b_english: Fifth proof (I put the rest off for another place). If the law threatened Adam with death as privation of righteousness, then—on your view—Adam died just as God had threatened. That looks false to me. First, you yourself, I take it, grant that Adam's first sin was forgiven; otherwise he would be counted among the damned. So he did not die just as God had threatened. Forgiveness of sin and punishment according to the law cannot both stand.

Second, by the death named in the threat you mean bodily death and eternal death as well as spiritual. Truth and justice in the threat would then require that on the very day he broke the law he die bodily, eternally, and spiritually. Yet that day he suffered neither bodily nor eternal death, and eternal death he never underwent and never will. Why could spiritual death's penalty not be forgiven Adam as eternal death's was—or at least deferred?
source_text: Quinta denique ratio, (caeteras enim differre, & in alium locum conferre satius erit.) Si lex Adamo mortem sitam in privatione justitiae comminabatur, Adamus (ut tu asseris) prout Deus minatus fuerat, Mortuus est. Id autem mihi falsum videtur. Nam primo, Tu, opinor, fateris Adamo condonatum fuisse primum illud peccatum, numerando alioquin inter damnatos: non igitur, prout Deus minatus fuerat, mortuus est. Pugnant enim haec duo, condonari peccatum & puniri secundum legem. Deinde, Tu per mortem denunciatam comminatione tam mortem corporis & aeternam intelligis, quam spiritualem illam. Pertinebat igitur aeque ad veritatem comminationis & justitiam, ut, quo die legem violavit, eodem tam corporea & aeterna morte, quam spirituali moreretur. Tamen eodem die neutram passus est, aeternam autem nunquam subiit, aut subibit. Cur non potuit Adamo mortis spiritualis aeque ac aeternae poena condonari? aut saltem differri?
